Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

This page collects, in Q&A form, the most common semantic and command-line questions when using SLA, covering variables and ownership, types, error handling, and the SAB build flow. After reading it, you can quickly judge whether a given form is legal in SLA and what form to use instead.

Variables, Assignment, and Ownership

Q: Are variables declared with let mutable by default?

Yes. In SLA, a let binding is mutable by default: a local binding can be reassigned, and fields/elements of an owned aggregate can also be updated when the value is usable. const is the immutable binding form. SLA does not introduce Rust-style mut, and there are no final/readonly keywords.

Q: After let b = a;, can a still be used?

It depends on the type. Integers, floats, booleans, and other scalars have copy semantics; small structs can use @derive(copy) so that let b = a; generates an independent field-by-field copy. For owned heap/resource values (such as Vec<T>), treat it as an ownership transfer — unless you clone explicitly, do not assume a deep copy or a cheap shared alias.

Q: After passing by value, can the caller still use its value?

A parameter of the form x: T is an owning/value parameter. It has no effect on scalars and copy-like values; for owned resource values, treat it as an ownership transfer. To keep the value, use a borrowing parameter x: &T or a return value instead. The explicit move operator is ^expr.

Q: Why are there no &mut and no lifetime annotations?

This is a design decision of the underlying SA language: shared reads and exclusive writes are decided dynamically by the SA Referee in the runtime context using bit masks (a borrowing view is marked exclusive when written, and a conflict traps directly), while cross-function borrow-graph tracking is the frontend's responsibility. At its current stage SLA introduces no mut form at all, and &self covers both reading and writing scenarios.

NoteMultiple writable aliases should not be assumed to be allowed. Alias constraints come from ownership/borrow tracking, runtime checks of interior-mutability types, and SA verification.

Types and the Syntax Surface

Q: What numeric types are there? Must conversions be explicit?

They include i8/i16/i32/i64/isize, u8/u16/u32/u64/usize, f32/f64, and the aliases int->i64, float->f64. Numeric conversions must use an explicit as; do not rely on implicit truncation or promotion.

Q: Is there a null? What encoding are strings?

There is no general null/nil value; absence is expressed with Option<T>/None. String facilities come from the SA std (String and slice-style APIs), and string literals are emitted as UTF-8 constants.

Q: Can functions be overloaded? Are there default parameters?

There is no general function overloading by signature, and no stably supported default parameters, named parameters, or variadic parameters; use different function names or generics instead. Operator overloading is supported only in the restricted form @overload Type { fn +(self: Type, other: Type) -> Type { ... } }, limited to + - * /, and is lowered at type-checking time to a static function call with no runtime dispatch overhead.

Q: Can match destructure enums?

Yes. match, if let, while let, and let ... else all support enum patterns, including common forms such as Some/None/Ok/Err. Note that lowering related to enum payload layout is still being refined; see the “Current Limitations and Roadmap Status” page in this chapter.

Error Handling and Runtime Behavior

Q: What do ? and panic(...) do?

The postfix ? is used for Option/Result-style error propagation; panic(...) lowers to SA panic behavior — in tests it is judged a failure unless annotated with @should_panic, and during normal execution it terminates the current execution. There is no general exception mechanism.

Q: Is there garbage collection or custom destructors?

There is no tracing GC. Cleanup is managed by the compiler: it inserts release instructions for live owned values at scope exits, branches, early returns, and loop boundaries, and then leaves it to the SA verifier to prove there are no leaks. There is no stable user-defined Drop trait surface; do cleanup via explicit functions or std/container APIs.

SAB Builds and Test Backends

Command / optionDescription
sla buildThe .sa text mainline path.
sla sab build / slab buildProduces a SAB artifact, written by default under .sla-cache/sab/.
--out <file.sab> / -oAdditionally writes a visible .sab file; workspaces use --sab-out, and --emit-sab generates a sibling .sab with the same name as the source file.
sla testDefaults to --test-backend auto: takes the SA text path (writes .test.sa) and hands it to sa test; when you need SAB, use --test-backend sab explicitly (opt-in).
sla init [path]Scaffolds a minimal binary project (sa.mod, src/main.sla, and writes .sla-cache/ into .gitignore).
TipThe commands in the table are all in the top-level sla command form; each has an equivalent sa sla … form (swap by removing the prefix), for example sla sab build is sa sla sab build. The top-level sla.exe is provided by the fully automatic installer or install_windows.ps1.
WarningOn the explicitly chosen SAB path, when the direct AST->SAB fast path does not yet cover a feature it errors loudly (UnsupportedSabDirectFeature) — the SA compatibility fallback has been removed and there is no silent fallback; the default SA text path (the production path) is not subject to this limit. For how to locate the problem, see the “Troubleshooting Build Failures” and “Performance and Optimization Expectations” pages in this chapter.
